tasks.entryDescription: Prüfer codes; Matrix-tree theorem/determinant; weighted generating functions.
tasks.currentSketch: Encode a labelled tree by repeatedly deleting its least-labelled leaf and recording its neighbor; after n−2 deletions the recorded labels form a word of length n−2. To invert, scan the word from left to right, joining its first entry to the least label not appearing in the remaining word, deleting that label and the first entry at each step; finally join the two remaining labels. The procedures are inverse, so labelled trees correspond bijectively to the n^(n−2) words.

tasks.currentSketch: For the complete graph K_n, every Laplacian cofactor counts spanning trees by the matrix-tree theorem. Its Laplacian cofactor has diagonal n−1 and off-diagonal −1; its eigenvalues are n (multiplicity n−2) and 1, so the determinant is n^(n−2).

tasks.entryDescription: Prüfer codes; Matrix-tree theorem/determinant; weighted generating functions.
tasks.currentSketch: Let T(x) count rooted labeled trees as an exponential generating function. Decomposing a rooted tree into its root and an unordered set of rooted branches gives T=x exp(T). Lagrange inversion yields [x^n]T=n^(n−1)/n!, so there are n^(n−1) rooted labeled trees; forgetting the choice of root divides by n and gives n^(n−2).

tasks.entryDescription: Alternating paths in maximum matchings; max-flow/min-cut; induction on tight subsets.
tasks.currentSketch: Take a maximum matching M. If some left vertex is unmatched, follow alternating paths (unmatched edges left-to-right, matched edges right-to-left). No reached right vertex can be unmatched, or there is an augmenting path. The reached left set has fewer neighbors than vertices, contradicting Hall.

tasks.entryDescription: Alternating paths in maximum matchings; max-flow/min-cut; induction on tight subsets.
tasks.currentSketch: Build a unit-capacity network: source to each left vertex, each bipartite edge left-to-right, and right vertices to sink. A flow of value |L| is a matching; max-flow/min-cut says this exists iff every cut has capacity ≥|L|, equivalent to |N(S)|≥|S| for each S⊆L.

tasks.entryDescription: Alternating paths in maximum matchings; max-flow/min-cut; induction on tight subsets.
tasks.currentSketch: Induct on |L|. If a proper nonempty S is tight, match S to N(S) by induction and match the remaining vertices in the reduced graph, whose Hall inequalities follow by applying Hall to S∪T. If no proper tight S exists, match any x to a neighbor y and remove both; strict inequalities ensure Hall remains.

tasks.entryDescription: Alternating-path construction; linear-programming duality/integrality; network-flow min-cut.
tasks.currentSketch: In a maximum matching, start from unmatched left vertices and trace alternating paths. Let Z_L,Z_R be reached vertices. Then C=(L\Z_L)∪Z_R meets every edge; each matched edge has exactly one endpoint in C, so |C|=|M|, proving vertex-cover minimum equals matching maximum.

tasks.entryName: König's theorem (bipartite vertex cover = maximum matching)
tasks.entryDescription: Alternating-path construction; linear-programming duality/integrality; network-flow min-cut.
tasks.currentSketch: Formulate bipartite matching as the LP maximizing Σ_e x_e subject to incident-edge sums at each vertex ≤1 and x≥0; the dual minimizes Σ_v y_v subject to y_u+y_v≥1 on each edge and y≥0. The bipartite incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so optimal basic solutions of both programs are integral. The integral primal solution is a matching and the integral dual solution is a vertex cover. Strong LP duality makes their cardinalities equal, proving König’s theorem.

tasks.entryDescription: Minimal-counterexample vertex of degree ≤5 plus recoloring; Kempe-chain argument; induction after contracting a configuration. *Proofs from THE BOOK* treats this.
tasks.routeTitle: Minimal-counterexample vertex of degree ≤5 plus recoloring
tasks.currentSketch: Choose a vertex v of degree at most five (Euler’s formula guarantees one), color G−v with five colors. If its five neighbors use all colors, relabel cyclically and consider the 1/3 Kempe chain from the first to third neighbor. If they connect, the 2/4 chain cannot connect without crossing; swap one chain and free a color. If they do not connect, swap the 1/3 component. Color v.

tasks.entryDescription: Minimal-counterexample vertex of degree ≤5 plus recoloring; Kempe-chain argument; induction after contracting a configuration. *Proofs from THE BOOK* treats this.
tasks.currentSketch: Use Kempe chains: among five differently colored neighbors around a degree-five vertex, if the 1-3 chain connecting the relevant opposite neighbors is absent, interchange colors in one component; if present, planarity prevents the 2-4 chain from joining the other pair, so interchange that component. One color becomes available. Details of cyclic neighbor order are essential.

tasks.currentSketch: For iid variables with mean μ and finite variance σ², Var(average)=σ²/n. Chebyshev gives P(|average−μ|≥ε)≤σ²/(nε²)→0, which is weak convergence in probability.

tasks.entryDescription: Chebyshev inequality and variance; characteristic functions; truncation plus Borel–Cantelli for stronger variants.
tasks.currentSketch: If φ is the characteristic function, finite variance implies φ(t)=1+iμt−σ²t²/2+o(t²). Thus [φ(t/√n)e^(−iμt/√n)]^n→e^(−σ²t²/2), a point mass at zero for the centered normalized average; continuity theorem yields convergence in probability (alternatively use φ near zero to bound tails). This is overkill versus Chebyshev; characteristic functions alone do not prove WLLN without a convergence theorem.

tasks.currentSketch: Use moments of normalized sums: expand each fixed moment; terms with singleton indices vanish and pairings dominate, yielding Gaussian moments. Tightness follows from bounded second moments; every subsequential limit has Gaussian moments, which determine the normal law.
